https://www.bostonglobe.com/2026/07/27/n.text: Tate brothers will remain in jail at least 2 more weeks as they fight extradition to the UK Andrew Tate, left in black, and his brother Tristan Tate, center rear, arrive at Fort Lauderdale-Hollywood International Airport in Florida on Feb. 27, 2025. JAMES JACKMAN/NYT Social media influencers Andrew and Tristan Tate will remain in jail at least two more weeks until their next hearing as they fight extradition to the United Kingdom, where the brothers are accused of rape and sex trafficking, a federal judge said Monday. U.S. Magistrate Lauren Louis set a detention hearing for Aug. 13 to determine whether the Tates should stay in jail or be released during what could be a monthslong extradition process. The brothers weren’t in court Monday or required to be there and have remained in jail since making a brief court appearance two days after their July 18 arrest. The Tates have become among the world’s most polarizing internet personalities with their promotion of wealth, male dominance and misogyny through their social media empire. The new allegations are the latest in a long-running international legal saga involving the Tates that has spanned the U.S., Britain and Romania. The brothers have repeatedly denied wrongdoing. Get Starting Point A guide through the most important stories of the morning, delivered Monday through Friday. Enter Email Sign Up Attorneys for the brothers said Monday that they want the U.S. government to turn over documents that U.K. officials submitted to secure their arrest. “They don’t have anything but the accusations,” attorney Joseph McBride said after the hearing. “It’s just their word against our word right now.” The U.K. has until mid-September to turn over all of its materials to the State Department, Assistant U.S. Attorney Alejandra López said in court. The brothers have long claimed that their violent and misogynistic statements have been taken out of context or were intended as jokes. Jackie Perczek, another one of their attorneys, said the Tates have shown they are not a flight risk by returning to Romania every month after they were accused there of luring women for sexual exploitation. “For three years they have not fled,” she said. “They’ve traveled the world and every month they return to Romania.” The former professional kickboxers, who have dual U.S. and U.K. citizenship, have millions of social media followers and are vocal supporters of President Donald Trump. The White House has said the brothers shouldn’t expect any help from the president. McBride said shortly after the Tates were arrested that “they’ve never done nothing wrong. They shouldn’t be extradited for crimes they did not commit,” he said. McBride said the extradition attempt was politically motivated, though he provided no details. Prosecutors in Britain said the new charges relate to four new accusers and were brought after authorities received evidence from police in Bedfordshire, in southeastern England. The allegations, which span from 2010 to 2017, include rape, assault, trafficking and offenses relating to “indecent images of a child and extreme pornography.” The brothers are already charged with rape, bodily harm, human trafficking and controlling prostitution for gain relating to three other accusers in the U.K. between 2012 and 2015. The brothers moved to Romania in 2016 and were arrested there in 2022, accused of participating in schemes to lure women for sexual exploitation. They denied those allegations, and the Romanian case hasn’t gone forward because of legal and procedural problems. Andrew Tate, 39, became known a decade ago when he was a contestant on the U.K. reality television show “Big Brother.” He was booted from the show when a video appeared to show him assaulting a woman. He has amassed over 10 million followers on X but has been banned from other platforms, including YouTube, TikTok and Instagram, for violating hate speech guidelines. He has made widely condemned comments, such as saying women who are sexually assaulted should bear some responsibility for the attacks and sharing graphic descriptions of how he might attack women.

https://us.cnn.com/2026/08/04/europe/fra.text: Hundreds of World War II shells and munitions have been discovered in the French village of Le Porge, as residents return to the ravaged community in the wake of last month’s blazes, according to local authorities. Explosions were heard near the village in France’s Gironde region following the devastating fires, which swept through the country’s southwest. “A bomb disposal operation was carried out today with Civil Protection specialists, recovering more than 400 shells and munitions,” a statement from the local authority said Monday. As the flames approached the community in July, the majority of the village’s 3,500 residents were forced to flee their homes, as hundreds of firefighters were deployed to tackle blazes more violent and unpredictable than in previous years. Temperatures in Central and Eastern Europe are soon expected to be 10 to 15 degrees Celsius (18 to 27 degrees Fahrenheit) above normal, as fires continue to spread in Greece and Italy. In Hungary, the country’s sole nuclear power station was “millimeters” away from shutting down early Tuesday due to low water levels in parts of the Danube River, Prime Minister Péter Magyar said. Elsewhere, Austria recorded its highest ever temperature on Tuesday at 40.8 degrees Celsius (105.4 degrees Fahrenheit), the country’s weather service said, citing a provisional measurement. Europe has always experienced wildfires, but scientists are clear that climate change is making them increasingly extreme. The fires in France have so far burned more than 160,000 hectares (about 617 square miles), making them the largest on record for the country. Upon returning to the scorched community, officials in Le Porge made a startling discovery. Despite World War II ending more than 80 years ago, unexploded munitions are still littered throughout the continent and frequently discovered or unearthed decades later. French President Emmanuel Macron said last month, “The situation we are dealing with today is the most severe we have ever recorded, the toughest since the Second World War.” “Following the fires, explosions were heard, and we responded last week, and we found this field and removed 75 shells,” commandant Philippe Delemotte, head of the Bordeaux bomb disposal unit, told French outlet France Info in an interview Monday. “Here, for instance, you’ve got two mortar shells, a French mortar shell and some German 5 (centimeter) shells,” he said. It is unclear why the munitions went undetected for so long, but Delemotte said the heat caused several of the buried shells to explode, alerting authorities to their location. Officials quickly established an exclusion zone due to the risk to the public, with Delemotte saying an explosion could potentially send “lethal fragments” flying several hundred meters through the air. ‘Everything burned’ On Monday, Gironde region’s prefect Sophie Brocas authorized residents to return to affected neighbourhoods after a safety assessment was conducted. Fires are still active in nearby coastal areas but remain “contained,” according to officials. Asked about the discovery of the wartime ammunition, Delemotte said authorities do “sometimes come across this, but it’s rare because here they’re scattered pretty much everywhere.” The French official said he believed the munitions were from historic demolition pits. Photos taken on Monday showed residents returning to the charred village and sifting through the remains of their burnt-out houses. A local resident told CNN last month that he lost his home and pets when the wildfire tore through Le Porge. “It was the apocalypse,” the resident said. “Everything burned, even the animals.” Across Europe, other historic objects have also been revealed this summer due to the record-breaking heat and crippling droughts hitting the continent’s waterways. Some of Europe’s rivers have shrunk to such a great extent that long-submerged relics from ancient bones to century-old shipwrecks have been revealed. In Hungary too, where the heat crisis is severely straining the country’s energy supply, the receding water levels of the Danube River exposed several bombs, likely from World War II, a local official said last week. Temperatures in the country are soon expected to reach 40 degrees Celsius (104 degrees Fahrenheit). The Hungarian Meteorological Service is forecasting Budapest to top out at 40 degrees Celsius for three consecutive days, something that has only occurred once before in the city’s recorded history, earlier this summer during the major European heatwave in late June. Magyar said Tuesday that Hungary may need to consider a different type of cooling system for the country’s Paks nuclear power plant, instead of relying on the Danube, Reuters reported. Water from the river is used to cool the plant’s reactor core and other crucial components.

https://www.theguardian.com/world/2026/s.text: Roberto Vannacci’s far-right Futuro Nazionale party has risen to about 8% in polls since its launch in February. Photograph: Remo Casilli/Reuters View image in fullscreen Roberto Vannacci’s far-right Futuro Nazionale party has risen to about 8% in polls since its launch in February. Photograph: Remo Casilli/Reuters Italy Analysis Rise of far-right leader Roberto Vannacci challenges Meloni as she celebrates Italian milestone Angela Giuffrida in Rome Futuro Nazionale party’s speedy poll rise poses questions whether PM will return to her roots before election Europe live – latest updates Thu 3 Sep 2026 10.25 EDT Last modified on Thu 3 Sep 2026 11.17 EDT Share Giorgia Meloni’s government has become the longest-running in Italy since the second world war – a milestone the prime minister is determined not to let pass unnoticed. In the port area of Bari, the capital of the southern Italian region of Puglia, where Meloni hosted the G7 in 2024 and where she spends her summer holiday, preparations are well under way for a festival-style showcase of her rightwing administration. On Friday, there will be food trucks, water stations and traditional Puglian light shows as part of celebrations to entertain an expected crowd of 10,000 people bussed in from across Italy . Militants from the youth wing of Meloni’s far-right Brothers of Italy party have fanned the city’s squares and beaches for days, handing out flyers promoting the celebrations while wearing T-shirts featuring the official slogan: Il Governo più stabile, l’Italia più forte (the most stable government, the strongest Italy). Meloni, who just a few weeks ago was booed at the opening ceremony of the Mediterranean Games in Taranto, farther south in Puglia, will address the audience in the evening, surrounded by her coalition allies – Matteo Salvini, the leader of the far-right League, and the conservative Forza Italia’s Antonio Tajani. “This moment will be written in the history books,” said Michele Picaro, a Brothers of Italy MEP and former Bari councillor. “We are the longest government in the history of the Italian Republic and this must be celebrated.” View image in fullscreen In recent months the political landscape has become less settled for Giorgia Meloni. Photograph: Francesca Bolla/AGF/Shutterstock Beneath the triumph, however, the outlook for Meloni is less settled. True, she has enjoyed a political stability that eluded her predecessors. Brothers of Italy is still the country’s biggest party. But in recent months, the political landscape has shifted with the emergence of a challenger – not from the left or the centre, but from someone who is even further to the right than Meloni. Since its launch in February, Roberto Vannacci, a former army general, has seen his far-right party, Futuro Nazionale, rise to about 8% in the polls, surpassing his former compatriots in the League months ago and this week eclipsing Forza Italia, too. Vannacci first entered the public eye in 2023 after self-publishing a book filled with racism, homophobia, Islamophobia and antisemitism. The subsequent backlash cost him his army job, but propelled him to the top of the bestsellers list. Helped along by ample coverage in the Italian press, he capitalised on the notoriety and in 2024 was elected as an MEP for the League, later leaving Salvini’s party to set up his own. “I read his book because I always think you need to know the enemy,” said Giulia Pastorella, an MP and vice-president of the small centrist party Azione (Action). “And I thought, this is exactly the kind of thing you might hear people talking about in the bar. Here’s a military man, who is really a mirror of the worst impulses of people. The scary thing is, I think he’s genuine and not a PR construct.” Vannacci’s policies, such as they are, are extreme. Futuro Nazionale’s recently published manifesto says that “abortion is not a right” and calls for gay people to be banned from TV between 6am and 11pm so children aren’t exposed to what it describes as “homosexualist” content. It also proposes introducing military education in high schools and a “remigration” plan to remove irregular immigrants and foreign nationals who commit crimes. On foreign policy, Vannacci has campaigned to stop weapons and financial aid to Ukraine, saying if he could choose between Vladimir Putin or the Ukrainian president, Volodymyr Zelenskyy, he would choose Putin . In July, he organised a “Futuristic Triathlon” in the northern seaside town of Sanremo, billed as an event to “temper the mind and body” in an echo of the fascist aesthetics and themes of the Mussolini era. View image in fullscreen Roberto Vannacci’s policies, such as they are, are extreme. Photograph: Remo Casilli/Reuters Far from being a treated as a pariah, however, Vannacci’s party has proved moderately successful, luring defectors from the three main ruling coalition parties. It is also actively courting disillusioned voters from the Five Star Movement, a key ally in a broad but perennially fractious leftwing coalition led by the Democratic party. For the government, he represents a dilemma. Meloni, whose Brothers of Italy has neofascist roots, has governed more moderately than many had expected, cultivating a pragmatic and, crucially, pro-Ukraine image abroad while still deploying hardline rhetoric on choice occasions for domestic audiences. skip past newsletter promotion Free newsletter | Weekly Sign up to This is Europe The most pressing stories and debates for Europeans – from identity to economics to the environment after newsletter promotion That positioning, however, has left a vacuum on the far right that Vannacci has exploited. The question now is: how will Meloni respond? Until now her ruling coalition had mostly coasted along, propped up by a strong parliamentary majority. Her government is largely regarded to have been fiscally prudent, but has steered clear of major structural reforms. Instead, it has heavily focused on security and continues to vigorously expand legislation on law and order . “This government has wasted the huge occasion that stability gave them,” said Lia Quartapelle, an MP with the Democratic party. “None of the core issues have been addressed – we have stagnant productivity and growth, salaries that have lagged behind for many years and an education system that is not up to the pace.” Pastorella said a focus on foreign policy had also contributed to Vannacci’s success. “Meloni hasn’t really done much at home but has been very present abroad,” she added. “The Italian electorate is tired of talking about foreign policy and would rather discuss national politics – this is precisely what Vannacci has understood.” Picaro batted away questions about recent polls. “This is a government that is more used to working than looking at percentages,” he said, citing lower unemployment, reduced irregular immigration, cutting taxes for the self-employed and an initiative in the south to boost entrepreneurial investment. Pastorella said that, far from being strong and stable, Meloni had struggled to keep her coalition united while dealing with various scandals, including ones that led to a tourism and a culture minister being forced to resign. With the possibility of an election as early as April, time is now of the essence for the prime minister. In recent weeks she has pivoted back to hardline rhetoric, most notably in her reaction to the influx of migrants from Morocco into the Spanish north African enclave of Ceuta. She is also trying to push through a highly contentious electoral law that would give a majority bonus to any alliance winning more than 42% of the vote, which critics say is aimed at increasing her group’s chance of victory. If Vannacci continues to strengthen, Meloni might be tempted to accommodate him before the vote, a move that would risk repelling moderate supporters. Or she could clinch a post-election pact to maintain power, resulting in what many both inside and outside Italy would see as a frightening shift to the extreme right. As government supporters head to Bari, Alessandro Cattaneo, an MP with Forza Italia, thinks it won’t come to that. “We in Forza Italia believe that Vannacci is too far removed from our political culture,” he said. “It would not be possible to govern with him … the coalition needs to continue to work seriously for the remainder of this administration and explain better to people what we have done. The best antidote to the extreme right is to show our seriousness.” Explore more on these topics Italy Giorgia Meloni Europe The far right news Share Reuse this content Most viewed Most viewed World Europe US news Americas Asia Australia Middle East Africa Inequality Global development

https://www.theguardian.com/world/2026/o.text: Donald Trump has twice rejected Saudi appeals for help. Photograph: Roberto Schmidt/Getty Images View image in fullscreen Donald Trump has twice rejected Saudi appeals for help. Photograph: Roberto Schmidt/Getty Images Yemen Analysis Houthi attack on Riyadh airport forces swift rethink of Trump’s new strategy Patrick Wintour US president’s plan to park the wars in Iran and Yemen, while blaming Ukraine for diesel prices, looks unsustainable Middle East crisis live - latest updates Sun 11 Oct 2026 09.23 EDT Last modified on Sun 11 Oct 2026 11.45 EDT Share The reckless missile attack on King Khalid international airport in Riyadh on Saturday did not just export the death and misery inside Yemen to Saudi Arabia, it also left Donald Trump forced to reconsider his diplomatic and political strategy designed to take him into the midterm elections next month. The US president’s plan had only been unveiled on Friday. He said it was the result of “a world problem” – spiralling diesel prices – which he blamed on Volodymyr Zelenskyy’s attacks on Russian oil refineries. He was going to keep the political temperature down on his war of choice in Iran and its spillover in Yemen until after the midterms. In pursuit of this strategy, he claimed the Iranian blockade in the strait of Hormuz was in effect broken, producing figures on daily oil barrel exports to assuage the markets. As a further insurance he also claimed it was impossible to negotiate with the Iranians since there was no single leadership in Tehran. Saudi Arabia, in conjunction with Turkey, and Pakistan, were largely to be left to sort out the Houthis along the Red Sea. The fate of Yemen, the poorest country in the world according to the International Monetary Fund, was not going to shift votes in Kansas or Alaska. Now, after the Riyadh airport attack, it is doubtful, for a basket of reasons, that this anyway threadbare strategy, largely born of desperation, can hold. For all the talk of the Gulf becoming responsible for its own security, it is doubtful that Saudi Arabia can be left to fend for itself after the carnage in Riyadh. One of the the 12 dead is an American and there may be more among the severely injured. Something is clearly wrong with Saudi defences since the Houthis are firing rockets from 500 miles away, and they are reaching their target too often. The US has had a unilateral ceasefire with the Houthis since 2025, and once the hostilities between Saudi Arabia and the Houthis recommenced in the summer, the pact was quietly renewed. Trump has twice rejected Saudi appeals for help. Can he spurn them three times? The pressure to act as allies are expected to may prove overwhelming. But “the blame Zelenskyy, trade with Russia” strategy is anyway unlikely to work. The amount of additional diesel Vladimir Putin will put on the market is not enough to bring down prices at the pump. Russia accounted for about 12% of global diesel shipped by sea. Exports have fallen by about a third, according to calculations by the Center for Research on Energy and Clean Air. The deal has also reawakened Europe’s worst fears about Trump’s relationship with Russia only weeks after Congress had passed a sanctions package against Moscow authorising Trump to penalise buyers of Russian energy. Europeans know full well that the inflation problem helping to drive populism is caused by the Iran war and not by Zelenskyy’s tactics. The only question is who will say so. The former UK Conservative prime minister Boris Johnson did not hold back, writing: “It is sickening that the USA is now lifting sanctions on Russian fuel, and transparently ridiculous to blame Ukraine for the spike in prices that obviously began with the closure of the strait of Hormuz. Putin is murdering innocent Ukrainian civilians every day. The Ukrainians are fighting for their lives. And yet the White House is apparently determined to force American drivers to bankroll Putin’s slaughter.” The German education minister and a member of the CDU, Karin Prien, said: “For a few litres of diesel. What moral bankruptcy.” Mark Rutte, the Nato secretary general and Trump ally, will this week travel to Estonia, one of the countries most supportive of Ukraine. He will have some explaining to do. Estonia’s foreign minister, Margus Tsahkna, vowed that EU foreign ministers on Monday will impose the biggest package of sanctions in its history, and he, along with Sweden, now wants to revisit using frozen Russian assets to help Ukraine. What is worse, it looks as if the political damage to the Republicans caused by the Iran war is irrecoverable. Polls show the ship has sailed. The war has already been weaponised as a pocketbook issue by every Democratic candidate in every TV debate. Republican candidates, challenged to disown the war, are scrambling for the relative safety of identity politics. The Iranians are also trying to maximise the damage they cause in the strait of Hormuz, countering the Trump narrative that the blockade has been broken. Scenes of tankers on fire are proliferating. So Trump post-Riyadh needs to rethink. He can rejoin the war against the Houthis, ending the unilateral US ceasefire, but, if so, he knows from experience this will be costly. The first three weeks of the war against Iran cost $1n a day. Many of the US president’s advisers say he may as well also attack Iran, the Houthis’ backers, as Tehran expects him to do. The Iranian military nevertheless still believes it has escalation dominance, and what happened in Riyadh can be repeated across the Gulf. The alternative is that his team can negotiate discreetly and indirectly with Tehran as is occurring in Doha. Some Iranians are urging their leadership to seize the chance, arguing Trump is uniquely vulnerable in the run-up to the midterms. A deal could be done, including on uranium enrichment, but it would not be palatable for the US – or for the Israeli prime minister, Benjamin Netanyahu’s re-election chances. China and Russia are trying to sort out the Houthis diplomatically, but the Houthi objectives are broadening, while the south of Yemen is split about its future inside the country, a division that harms the country’s ability to be the ground component that Saudi Arabia needs to supplement its air-power dominance. Taiz, the third city of Yemen, is struggling to overcome a Houthi siege. The Saudis can deliver retribution, but retribution is not a solution to a decade-long civil war. So for the moment the twin Trump strategy – to park the Iran and Yemen conflicts while blaming Zelenskyy – is now so transparent, so morally craven, and in its own terms so ineffective, that it looks unsustainable. The only question is whether the strategy will be jettisoned by the president or instead just rejected by the American people at the ballot box. https://www.dw.com/en/canada-major-fire-.text: Skip to content Skip to main menu Skip to more DW sites https://p.dw.com/p/5ON8t Carney said 'our thoughts are with all the brave women and men affected' [FILE: September 13, 2026] Image: Jon Blacker/The Canadian Press/PA Images/picture alliance Advertisement Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney on Saturday said a "serious incident" sparked a major fire at a military base in Alberta. "A serious incident creating a major fire has occurred at CFB Wainwright, in Alberta," Carney said in a post on X. He added that the federal government was working closely with Alberta officials and local authorities. What else do we know about the major fire in Alberta? Alberta Premier Danielle Smith called the fire "significant and tragic" and said many military personnel are affected. "We are learning of a significant and tragic fire at CFB Wainwright today that is affecting many of our brave military personnel," Smith said in a post on social media. Neither Carney nor Smith provided details on the cause of the fire or whether anyone was injured. The incident occurred just days before people in Alberta, home to the world's fourth-largest proven oil reserves, will vote in the October 19 referendum on whether the province wants to begin the process of separating from the rest of Canada .
